title: V. The Grand Inquisitor
paragraphs: “Even this needs a preface—a literary one, I mean,” Ivan laughed, “and I’m no good at writing them. My story is set in the sixteenth century. In those days, as you probably learned at school, poets liked to bring heavenly powers down to earth. Leave Dante aside. In France, clerks and the monks in the monasteries put on regular plays that brought the Madonna, the saints, the angels, Christ, and God himself onto the stage. It was all done quite simply then. In Victor Hugo’s _Notre Dame de Paris_, the people of Paris are treated to a free, edifying spectacle in the Hôtel de Ville, in the reign of Louis XI., to mark the birth of the dauphin. It was called _Le bon jugement de la très sainte et gracieuse Vierge Marie_, and the Virgin herself appears on the stage and delivers her _bon jugement_. Plays like this, mostly from the Old Testament, were staged in Moscow now and then too, right up to the time of Peter the Great. Besides plays, legends and ballads went around the world in which saints, angels and all the powers of Heaven took part whenever they were needed. In our monasteries the monks busied themselves translating, copying, even composing such poems—and they did it even under the Tatars. One such poem (from the Greek, naturally) is _The Wanderings of Our Lady through Hell_, with descriptions as bold as Dante’s. Our Lady goes down to hell, and the Archangel Michael guides her through the torments. She sees the sinners and their punishment. Among them she sees one remarkable group in a burning lake. Some of them sink to the bottom and can’t swim out again, and ‘these God forgets’—an expression of extraordinary depth and force. Shocked and weeping, Our Lady falls before the throne of God and begs mercy for everyone in hell, for all she has seen there, without distinction. Her conversation with God is immensely interesting. She pleads with Him and will not give way. When God points to the hands and feet of her Son, nailed to the Cross, and asks, ‘How can I forgive His tormentors?’ she calls on all the saints, all the martyrs, all the angels and archangels to fall down with her and beg mercy for all without distinction. In the end she wins from God a respite from suffering every year from Good Friday until Trinity Day. The sinners at once cry out their thanks from hell, chanting, ‘You are just, O Lord, in this judgment.’ Well, my poem would have been of that kind if it had come out in that age. He appears in my poem, but He says nothing. He only appears and passes on. Fifteen centuries have gone by since He promised to come in His glory. Fifteen centuries have gone by since His prophet wrote, ‘Behold, I come quickly’; and ‘Of that day and that hour knoweth no man, neither the Son, but the Father,’ as He Himself foretold on earth. But humanity waits for Him with the same faith and the same love. Oh, with greater faith, in fact, for fifteen centuries have passed since man stopped seeing signs from heaven.
No signs from heaven come today To add to what the heart does say.

There was nothing left but faith in what the heart says. It is true that there were many miracles in those days. Some saints performed miraculous cures. Some holy people, according to their biographies, were visited by the Queen of Heaven herself. But the devil never slept, and people were already beginning to doubt that these miracles were true. Just then a terrible new heresy appeared in the north of Germany. “A huge star like a torch” (that is, a church) “fell on the sources of the waters, and they became bitter.” These heretics began blasphemously to deny miracles. But the faithful who remained burned all the more ardently. The tears of humanity went up to Him as before. They awaited His coming, loved Him, hoped for Him, and longed to suffer and die for Him, as before. For so many ages mankind had prayed with faith and fervor, “O Lord our God, hasten Your coming.” So many ages they had called upon Him that in His infinite mercy He chose to come down to His servants. He had come down before that day, too. He had visited some holy men, martyrs and hermits, as their lives record. Among us, Tyutchev, in absolute faith in the truth of his words, bore witness that
Bearing the Cross, in a slave’s dress, Weary and worn, the King of Heaven came To bless our mother Russia, and through our land went wandering.
And it certainly was so, I assure you.

“And so He chose to show Himself for a moment to the people—the tortured, suffering people, sunk in iniquity yet loving Him like children. My story is set in Spain, in Seville, in the most terrible time of the Inquisition. Fires were lit every day then to the glory of God, and ‘in the splendid _auto da fé_ the wicked heretics were burnt.’ Oh, of course, this was not the coming in which He will appear, as He promised, at the end of time in all His heavenly glory—the one that will be sudden, ‘as lightning flashing from east to west.’ No, He visited His children only for a moment, and just where the flames were crackling around the heretics. In His infinite mercy He came once more among men in the human shape in which He had walked among them for three years, fifteen centuries before. He came down to the ‘hot pavements’ of a southern town. The day before, in that town, almost a hundred heretics had been burnt, _ad majorem gloriam Dei_, by the cardinal, the Grand Inquisitor, in a magnificent _auto da fé_. The king was there, and the court, the knights, the cardinals, the loveliest ladies of the court, and the whole population of Seville.

“He came softly and unnoticed, and yet—strange to say—everyone recognized Him. This might be one of the best passages in the poem: I mean, the reason why they recognized Him. The people are drawn to Him irresistibly. They crowd around Him, throng about Him, follow Him. He moves silently among them, with a gentle smile of infinite compassion. The sun of love burns in His heart. Light and power shine from His eyes, and their radiance falls on the people and stirs their hearts to answering love. He stretches out His hands to them and blesses them, and a healing virtue goes out from touching Him, even from touching His clothes. An old man in the crowd, blind since childhood, cries out, ‘O Lord, heal me, and I will see You!’ and something like scales falls from his eyes, and the blind man sees Him. The crowd weeps and kisses the ground beneath His feet. Children throw flowers in His path, sing, and cry hosannah. ‘It is He—it is He!’ they all say. ‘It must be He; it can be no one but Him!’ He stops on the steps of the Seville cathedral just as some weeping mourners are bringing in a small open white coffin. In it lies a child of seven, the only daughter of a prominent citizen. The dead child is hidden in flowers. ‘He will raise your child,’ the crowd calls to the weeping mother. The priest who comes out to meet the coffin looks perplexed and frowns. But the dead child’s mother throws herself at His feet with a wail. ‘If it is You, raise my child!’ she cries, holding out her hands to Him. The procession halts, and the coffin is set down on the steps at His feet. He looks on with compassion, and His lips once more softly say, ‘Maiden, arise!’ And the maiden arises. The little girl sits up in the coffin and looks about her, smiling, with wide, wondering eyes. She is holding the bunch of white roses they had put in her hand.

“There are cries and sobs and confusion among the people, and at that moment the cardinal himself, the Grand Inquisitor, passes the cathedral. He is an old man of almost ninety, tall and straight, with a withered face and sunken eyes, in which a gleam of light still shines. He is not in the gorgeous cardinal’s robes he wore the day before, when he was burning the enemies of the Roman Church. Now he wears his coarse old monk’s cassock. His gloomy assistants and slaves and the ‘holy guard’ follow at a distance. He stops when he sees the crowd and watches from afar. He sees everything. He sees them set the coffin down at His feet, sees the child rise up, and his face darkens. He knits his thick gray brows, and his eyes gleam with a sinister fire. He points his finger and orders the guards to seize Him. Such is his power, and so completely are the people cowed into trembling obedience to him, that the crowd at once makes way for the guards. In deathlike silence they lay hands on Him and lead Him away. The crowd bows to the ground at once, like one man, before the old Inquisitor. He blesses the people in silence and moves on. The guards take their prisoner to a narrow, gloomy, vaulted cell in the ancient palace of the Holy Inquisition and lock Him in. The day passes, and the dark, burning, ‘breathless’ night of Seville comes. The air is ‘fragrant with laurel and lemon.’ In the pitch darkness the iron door of the cell is suddenly opened, and the Grand Inquisitor himself comes in, carrying a light. He is alone. The door is shut behind him at once. He stands in the doorway and for a minute or two looks into His face. At last he walks slowly up to Him, puts the light down on the table, and speaks.

“‘Is it You? You?’ He gets no answer and adds at once, ‘Do not answer; be silent. What could You say, after all? I know only too well what You would say. And You have no right to add anything to what You said of old. Why have You come to stand in our way? For You have come to stand in our way, and You know it. But do You know what tomorrow will bring? I do not know who You are, and I do not care to know whether it is You or only a semblance of Him. But tomorrow I will condemn You and burn You at the stake as the worst of heretics. And these same people who kissed Your feet today will rush tomorrow, at the faintest sign from me, to heap the embers on Your fire. Do You know that? Yes, perhaps You do,’ he added with thoughtful insight, never for a moment taking his eyes off the Prisoner.”

“I don’t quite understand, Ivan. What does it mean?” said Alyosha, who had been listening in silence, with a smile. “Is it just a wild fantasy, or some mistake on the old man’s part—some impossible _quiproquo_?”

“Take it as the last one,” said Ivan, laughing, “if modern realism has so corrupted you that you can’t stand anything fantastic. If you want it to be a case of mistaken identity, let it be. It is true,” he went on, laughing, “the old man was ninety, and he might well have gone mad over his fixed idea. The appearance of the Prisoner might have struck him. It might, in fact, be simply his ravings, the delusion of a ninety-year-old man, overexcited by the _auto da fé_ of a hundred heretics the day before. But does it matter to us, after all, whether it was mistaken identity or a wild fantasy? All that matters is that the old man should speak out, should speak openly of what he has thought in silence for ninety years.”
“And the Prisoner is silent too? Does He look at him and not say a word?”

“That’s inevitable in any case,” Ivan laughed again. “The old man has told Him He has no right to add anything to what He said of old. You could say this is the most basic feature of Roman Catholicism, in my opinion at least. ‘Everything was handed over by You to the Pope,’ they say, ‘so everything still rests in the Pope’s hands, and You have no need to come at all now. You must not interfere, at least for the time being.’ That is how they talk and write—the Jesuits, at any rate. I have read it myself in their theologians’ works. ‘Have You the right to reveal to us even one of the mysteries of the world from which You have come?’ my old man asks Him, and answers the question for Him. ‘No, You have not. You may not add to what has been said of old, and You may not take from men the freedom that You exalted when You were on earth. Anything new that You reveal will infringe on men’s freedom of faith, because it will be plain as a miracle, and the freedom of their faith was dearer to You than anything in those days, fifteen hundred years ago. Did You not often say then, “I will make you free”? But now You have seen these “free” men,’ the old man suddenly adds, with a pensive smile. ‘Yes, we have paid dearly for it,’ he goes on, looking sternly at Him. ‘But at last we have finished that work in Your name. For fifteen centuries we have struggled with Your freedom, and now it is over and done with for good. Do You not believe it is done with for good? You look at me meekly and do not even deign to be angry with me. But let me tell You: today, more than ever, people are convinced that they have perfect freedom, and yet they have brought us their freedom and laid it humbly at our feet. That was our doing. Was this what You did? Was this Your freedom?’”
“I don’t understand again,” Alyosha broke in. “Is he being ironical, is he joking?”

“Not a bit of it! He claims it as a merit for himself and his Church that they have at last conquered freedom, and done it to make men happy. ‘For now’ (he means the Inquisition, of course) ‘for the first time, it has become possible to think about men’s happiness. Man was made a rebel, and how can rebels be happy? You were warned,’ he tells Him. ‘You had no lack of admonitions and warnings, but You did not heed them. You rejected the one way by which men could be made happy. But luckily, when You left, You passed the work on to us. You promised it, You confirmed it by Your word, You gave us the right to bind and to unbind. So of course You cannot now think of taking it away. Why, then, have You come to stand in our way?’”
“And what does ‘no lack of admonitions and warnings’ mean?” asked Alyosha.
“Why, that’s the main part of what the old man has to say.

“‘The wise and dread spirit, the spirit of self-destruction and non-existence,’ the old man goes on, ‘the great spirit spoke with You in the wilderness. The books tell us he “tempted” You. Is that so? Could anything truer be said than what he put to You in three questions—the questions You rejected, which the books call “the temptation”? And yet, if a truly stupendous miracle has ever happened on earth, it happened on that day, the day of the three temptations. The very putting of those three questions was the miracle. Imagine, just for the sake of argument, that those three questions of the dread spirit had vanished completely from the books, and we had to restore them and invent them anew. To do so we would gather all the wise men of the earth—rulers, chief priests, scholars, philosophers, poets—and set them the task of inventing three questions. These would have to suit the occasion, and also express in three words, three human phrases, the whole future history of the world and of humanity. Do You believe that all the wisdom of the earth, united, could have invented anything equal in depth and force to the three questions that the wise and mighty spirit actually put to You then in the wilderness? From those questions alone, from the miracle of their being put, we can see that we are dealing not with a passing human intelligence but with the absolute and the eternal. For those three questions gather the whole later history of mankind, as it were, into one, and foretell it, and in them all the unsolved historical contradictions of human nature are united. At the time this could not be so clear, since the future was unknown. But now, after fifteen hundred years, we see that everything in those three questions was so rightly divined and foretold, and has been so truly fulfilled, that nothing can be added to them or taken away.

“‘Judge for Yourself who was right, You or the one who questioned You then. Remember the first question. Its meaning, put another way, was this: “You are going into the world with empty hands, with some promise of freedom that men, in their simplicity and natural unruliness, cannot even understand, that they fear and dread—for nothing has ever been more unbearable to a man or a human society than freedom. But do You see these stones in this parched and barren wilderness? Turn them into bread, and mankind will run after You like a flock of sheep, grateful and obedient, though forever trembling that You might withdraw Your hand and deny them Your bread.” But You would not take freedom from man. You rejected the offer, thinking, what is that freedom worth if obedience is bought with bread? You answered that man does not live by bread alone. But do You know that for the sake of that earthly bread the spirit of the earth will rise against You, and fight You, and overcome You? All will follow him, crying, “Who can compare with this beast? He has given us fire from heaven!” Do You know that ages will pass, and humanity will declare through the lips of its sages that there is no crime and therefore no sin, only hunger? “Feed men, and then ask virtue of them!” That is what they will write on the banner they will raise against You, and with which they will destroy Your temple. A new building will rise where Your temple stood. The terrible tower of Babel will be built again. Like the old one, it will not be finished, yet You could have prevented that new tower and cut men’s sufferings short by a thousand years. For they will come back to us after a thousand years of agony with their tower. They will look for us again, hidden underground in the catacombs, for we will again be persecuted and tortured. They will find us and cry out to us, “Feed us, for those who promised us fire from heaven have not given it!” And then we will finish building their tower, for whoever feeds them finishes the building. And we alone will feed them in Your name, and we will falsely claim that it is in Your name. Oh, never, never can they feed themselves without us! No science will give them bread as long as they remain free. In the end they will lay their freedom at our feet and say to us, “Make us your slaves, but feed us.” At last they will understand for themselves that freedom and enough bread for all cannot go together, for never, never will they be able to share it among themselves! They will also be convinced that they can never be free, because they are weak, vicious, worthless and rebellious. You promised them the bread of Heaven. But, I repeat, can it compare with earthly bread in the eyes of the weak, ever sinful and ignoble race of man? And suppose thousands follow You for the sake of the bread of Heaven. What is to become of the millions, the tens of thousands of millions, of creatures who will not have the strength to give up earthly bread for the heavenly? Or do You care only for the tens of thousands of the great and strong, while the millions, as many as the sands of the sea, who are weak but love You, must exist only for the sake of the great and strong? No, we care for the weak too. They are sinful and rebellious, but in the end they will become obedient too. They will marvel at us and take us for gods, because we are ready to bear the freedom they found so dreadful, and to rule over them—so awful will it seem to them to be free. But we will tell them that we are Your servants and that we rule them in Your name. We will deceive them again, for we will not let You come to us again. That deception will be our suffering, for we will be forced to lie.

“‘That is what the first question in the wilderness meant. That is what You turned down, for the sake of the freedom You placed above everything else. Yet the great secret of this world lies hidden in that question. Had You chosen “bread,” You would have satisfied the universal and everlasting craving of all humanity—the craving to find someone to worship. A man who is free has no goal he pursues so restlessly and so painfully as this: to find someone to worship. But he wants to worship something no one can dispute, something so plainly established that all men would agree at once to bow to it. These pitiful creatures are not satisfied to find what this man or that man can worship. They must find something that everyone will believe in and worship, and above all they must do it _together_. This craving for worship in _common_ has been the chief misery of each man, and of the whole race, since time began. For the sake of common worship they have put each other to the sword. They have set up gods and challenged one another: “Put away your gods and come and worship ours, or we will kill you and your gods!” So it will be until the end of the world, even when the gods have vanished from the earth. They will fall down before idols all the same. You knew this basic secret of human nature. You could not help knowing it. Yet You refused the one sure banner that was held out to You, the banner that would have made every man bow down to You alone—the banner of earthly bread. You refused it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. Now see what You did next. And again, all of it in the name of freedom! I tell You, no anxiety torments man more than the need to find, and quickly, someone to whom he can hand over the gift of freedom with which the poor creature is born. But only one who can quiet their conscience can take their freedom from them. In bread You were offered a banner nothing could beat: give men bread and they will worship You, because nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gets hold of man’s conscience—oh! then he will throw away Your bread and follow the one who has trapped his conscience. In that You were right. The secret of man’s existence is not just to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm idea of what he lives for, man would not agree to go on living. He would rather destroy himself than stay on earth, even with bread in plenty. That is true. But what came of it? Instead of taking men’s freedom away, You made it greater than ever! Did You forget that man prefers peace, even death, to the freedom of choosing in the knowledge of good and evil? Nothing tempts man more than his freedom of conscience, and nothing makes him suffer more. And now see: instead of building a firm foundation to put man’s conscience at rest for ever, You chose everything that is exceptional, vague and puzzling. You chose what was wholly beyond men’s strength, and acted as though You did not love them at all—You, who came to give Your life for them! Instead of taking over men’s freedom, You added to it. You loaded the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its sufferings for ever. You wanted man’s love given freely. You wanted him to follow You freely, drawn and made captive by You. In place of the rigid ancient law, man would now have to decide for himself, with a free heart, what is good and what is evil, with only Your image before him as a guide. But did You not know that in the end he would reject even Your image and Your truth, once the fearful burden of free choice weighed him down? In the end they will cry out that the truth is not in You. They could not have been left in worse confusion and torment than You have left them in, piling on them so many cares and so many problems that have no answer.

“‘So in truth You Yourself laid the foundation for the ruin of Your own kingdom, and no one is more to blame. And yet, what was it that You were offered? There are three powers, only three, that can conquer for ever the conscience of these helpless rebels and hold it captive, for their own happiness. Those forces are miracle, mystery and authority. You rejected all three, and You gave the example for rejecting them. The wise and dread spirit set You on the pinnacle of the temple and said to You, “If You would know whether You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down. For it is written: the angels shall hold him up so that he does not fall and hurt himself. Then You will know whether You are the Son of God, and You will have shown how great Your faith in Your Father is.” But You refused. You would not throw Yourself down. Oh, of course, You acted proudly and nobly, like God. But the weak, unruly race of men—are they gods? Oh, You knew then that if You took a single step, made a single move to throw Yourself down, You would be tempting God and would lose all Your faith in Him. You would be smashed against the very earth You came to save. And the wise spirit who tempted You would have been delighted. But I ask again: are there many like You? Could You believe for a single moment that men, too, could stand up to such a temptation? Is human nature made so that men can turn down miracle? In the great moments of their lives, the moments of their deepest and most agonizing spiritual struggle, can they hold only to the free verdict of the heart? Oh, You knew that Your deed would be written down in books and handed on to distant ages and to the farthest ends of the earth. You hoped that man, following You, would hold to God and ask for no miracle. But You did not know that when man rejects miracle, he rejects God as well. Man looks not so much for God as for the miraculous. And since he cannot bear to be without the miraculous, he will make new miracles for himself. He will worship acts of sorcery and witchcraft, even if he is a hundred times a rebel, a heretic and an infidel. You did not come down from the Cross when they shouted at You, mocking and insulting You, “Come down from the cross and we will believe that You are He.” You did not come down. Again You would not make man a slave by a miracle. You longed for faith given freely, not faith founded on miracle. You longed for free love, not for the base raptures of a slave before a power that has terrified him for good. But in this You thought too highly of men. They are slaves, of course, though rebels by nature. Look around and judge. Fifteen centuries have gone by; look at them. Who have You raised up to Yourself? I swear, man is weaker and baser by nature than You believed! Can he, can he do what You did? You showed him so much respect that You seemed to stop feeling for him, for You asked far too much of him—You, who have loved him more than Yourself! Had You respected him less, You would have asked less of him. That would have been closer to love, because his burden would have been lighter. He is weak and vile. So what if he is now in revolt everywhere against our power, and proud of his revolt? That is the pride of a child, of a schoolboy. They are little children rioting and locking the teacher out of the classroom. But their childish delight will come to an end, and it will cost them dearly. They will pull down temples and soak the earth in blood. But in the end they will see, the foolish children, that though they are rebels, they are rebels without strength, who cannot even keep their own rebellion going. Drenched in their foolish tears, they will recognize at last that He who made them rebels must have meant to mock them. They will say so in despair, and what they say will be blasphemy, which will make them more unhappy still. For man’s nature cannot bear blasphemy, and always ends by taking its revenge on itself. And so: unrest, confusion and unhappiness—that is the lot of man today, after all You suffered for the sake of their freedom! The great prophet tells, in vision and in image, that he saw all those who shared in the first resurrection, and that there were twelve thousand from each tribe. But if there were so many, they must have been not men but gods. They had carried Your cross. They had lasted scores of years in the barren, hungry wilderness, living on locusts and roots. And You may indeed point with pride to those children of freedom, of free love, of free and glorious sacrifice for Your name. But remember that they were only a few thousand. And what of the rest? How are the other weak ones to blame, because they could not endure what the strong endured? How is the weak soul to blame, if it cannot take in such terrible gifts? Can You really have come only to the elect, and only for the elect? But if so, that is a mystery, and we cannot understand it. And if it is a mystery, then we too have the right to preach a mystery. We have the right to teach them that what counts is not the free judgment of their hearts, and not love, but a mystery that they must follow blindly, even against their conscience. That is what we have done. We have corrected Your work and built it on _miracle_, _mystery_ and _authority_. And men were glad to be led like sheep again, and glad that the terrible gift that had brought them such suffering was at last lifted from their hearts. Were we right to teach them this? Speak! Did we not love mankind, when we humbly admitted its feebleness, lovingly lightened its burden, and, with our sanction, let its weak nature sin? Why have You come now to get in our way? And why do You look at me so silently and so searchingly with Your gentle eyes? Be angry. I do not want Your love, for I do not love You. And what is the use of hiding anything from You? Do I not know Whom I am talking to? Everything I can say is already known to You. And is it for me to hide our mystery from You? Perhaps You wish to hear it from my own lips. Listen, then. We are not working with You, but with _him_—that is our mystery. It is a long time now—eight centuries—that we have been on _his_ side and not on Yours. Exactly eight centuries ago, we took from him what You rejected with scorn: the last gift he offered You, when he showed You all the kingdoms of the earth. From him we took Rome and the sword of Cæsar, and we declared ourselves the only rulers of the earth, though to this day we have not managed to finish our work. But whose fault is that? Oh, the work is only beginning, but it has begun. It will be a long time before it is done, and the earth still has much to suffer. But we shall triumph and be Cæsars, and then we shall plan the happiness of all mankind. Yet You could have taken the sword of Cæsar even then. Why did You reject that last gift? If You had accepted the mighty spirit’s last advice, You would have achieved everything man looks for on earth. That is, someone to worship, someone to keep his conscience, and some way of uniting everyone in one agreed and harmonious ant-heap. For the craving for universal unity is the third and last torment of men. Mankind as a whole has always struggled to set up a world state. There have been many great nations with great histories. But the more highly developed they were, the more unhappy they were, because they felt the craving for world-wide union more sharply than other peoples. The great conquerors, the Timours and Ghenghis-Khans, swept over the face of the earth like hurricanes, trying to subdue its peoples. They too were only the unconscious expression of that same craving for universal unity. If You had taken the world and Cæsar’s purple, You would have founded the universal state and given the world peace. For who can rule men, if not the one who holds their conscience and their bread in his hands? We have taken the sword of Cæsar. In taking it, of course, we have rejected You and followed _him_. Oh, there are ages still to come of confused free thought, of their science and their cannibalism. For they began to build their tower of Babel without us, and they will end, of course, in cannibalism. But then the beast will crawl to us, lick our feet and spatter them with tears of blood. And we shall sit upon the beast and raise the cup, and on it will be written, “Mystery.” But then, and only then, the reign of peace and happiness will come for men. You are proud of Your elect, but You have only the elect, while we give rest to all. And besides, how many of those elect, those mighty ones who might have become elect, have grown tired of waiting for You? They have carried, and will carry, the strength of their spirit and the warmth of their heart over to the other camp, and they end by raising their _free_ banner against You. You Yourself lifted up that banner. But with us everyone will be happy. They will no longer rebel or destroy one another, as they do under Your freedom. Oh, we shall persuade them that they will become free only when they give up their freedom to us and submit to us. And will we be right, or will we be lying? They will be convinced that we are right. They will remember the horrors of slavery and confusion to which Your freedom brought them. Freedom, free thought and science will lead them into such difficulties, and bring them face to face with such wonders and unsolvable mysteries, that some of them, the fierce and rebellious, will destroy themselves. Others, rebellious but weak, will destroy one another. The rest, weak and unhappy, will crawl to our feet, fawning, and whine to us: “Yes, you were right, you alone possess His mystery, and we come back to you, save us from ourselves!”

“‘When they receive bread from us, they will see plainly that we take the bread their own hands have made, only to hand it back to them, and that there is no miracle in it. They will see that we do not turn stones into bread. Yet in truth they will be more grateful for receiving it from our hands than for the bread itself! They will remember only too well that in the old days, without our help, even the bread they made turned to stones in their hands, while since they came back to us, the very stones have turned to bread in their hands. Too, too well will they understand the value of complete submission! And until men understand that, they will be unhappy. Who is most to blame that they do not? Speak! Who scattered the flock and sent it wandering down unknown paths? But the flock will gather again and submit once more, and this time it will be for good. Then we shall give them the quiet, humble happiness of weak creatures, which is what they are by nature. Oh, we shall persuade them in the end not to be proud, because You lifted them up and so taught them pride. We shall show them that they are weak, that they are nothing but pitiful children, and that a child’s happiness is the sweetest there is. They will grow timid. They will look to us and press close to us in fear, as chicks do to the hen. They will marvel at us and stand in awe of us. They will take pride in our being so powerful and so clever that we could tame a flock this unruly, thousands of millions strong. They will tremble helplessly before our wrath, their minds will fill with fear, and they will cry as easily as women and children do. But at a sign from us they will turn just as readily to laughter and rejoicing, to happy mirth and childish song. Yes, we shall make them work, but in their free hours we shall arrange their life like a child’s game, with children’s songs and innocent dances. Oh, we shall even let them sin. They are weak and helpless, and they will love us like children because we let them sin. We shall tell them that every sin will be atoned for if it is done with our permission. We let them sin because we love them, we shall say, and the punishment for these sins we take on ourselves. And we shall take it on ourselves, and they will adore us as the saviors who have borne their sins before God. They will keep no secrets from us. We shall permit or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, and to have children or not, depending on whether they have obeyed or disobeyed, and they will submit to us gladly and cheerfully. The most painful secrets of their conscience, all, all of them, they will bring to us, and we shall have an answer for all. They will be glad to believe our answer, for it will spare them the great anxiety and the terrible agony they suffer now, having to decide freely for themselves. And all will be happy, all the millions of creatures, except the hundred thousand who rule over them. For only we, who guard the mystery, will be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy babes, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken on themselves the curse of the knowledge of good and evil. Peacefully they will die, peacefully they will expire in Your name, and beyond the grave they will find nothing but death. But we shall keep the secret, and for their happiness we shall tempt them on with the reward of heaven and eternity. Though if there were anything in the other world, it certainly would not be for such as they. It is prophesied that You will come again in victory, with Your chosen, the proud and the strong. But we will say that they have saved only themselves, and we have saved everyone. We are told that the harlot who sits upon the beast, holding the _mystery_ in her hands, will be put to shame; that the weak will rise up again, tear her royal purple, and strip her loathsome body bare. But then I will stand up and show You the thousand millions of happy children who have never known sin. And we, who took their sins on ourselves for their happiness, will stand before You and say: “Judge us, if You can and dare.” Know that I do not fear You. Know that I too have been in the wilderness, that I too lived on roots and locusts, that I too prized the freedom You have blessed men with, and that I too was struggling to take my place among Your elect, among the strong and mighty, hungering “to make up the number.” But I woke up, and I refused to serve madness. I turned back and joined the ranks of those _who have corrected Your work_. I left the proud and returned to the humble, for the happiness of the humble. What I tell You will come to pass, and our dominion will be built. I repeat, tomorrow You will see that obedient flock, which at one sign from me will rush to pile the glowing coals around the stake where I shall burn You for coming to hinder us. For if anyone has ever deserved our fires, it is You. Tomorrow I shall burn You. _Dixi._’”
Ivan stopped. He had been carried away as he talked, and had spoken with great excitement. When he had finished, he suddenly smiled.
Alyosha had listened in silence. Toward the end he was deeply moved and seemed several times on the point of interrupting, but held himself back. Now his words came in a rush.

“But... that’s absurd!” he cried, flushing. “Your poem praises Jesus, it doesn’t blame Him—though you meant it to. And who will believe you about freedom? Is that how it should be understood? That’s not the idea of it in the Orthodox Church.... That’s Rome, and not even the whole of Rome, it’s false—those are the worst of the Catholics, the Inquisitors, the Jesuits!... And there could never be a fantastic creature like your Inquisitor. What are these sins of mankind that they take on themselves? Who are these keepers of the mystery, who have taken some curse upon themselves for the happiness of mankind? When has anyone seen them? We know the Jesuits. People speak ill of them, but surely they are not what you describe? They are not that at all, not at all.... They are simply the Roman army for the earthly rule of the world in the future, with the Pontiff of Rome for Emperor... that’s their ideal, but there’s no kind of mystery or lofty sadness about it.... It’s plain lust for power, for filthy earthly gain, for domination—something like a universal serfdom with them as the masters—that’s all they stand for. Perhaps they don’t even believe in God. Your suffering Inquisitor is a pure fantasy.”

“Wait, wait,” laughed Ivan, “how worked up you are! A fantasy, you say. Fine, let it be one! Of course it’s a fantasy. But let me ask you: do you really think the Roman Catholic movement of the last centuries is nothing but lust for power, for filthy earthly gain? Is that what Father Païssy teaches?”
“No, no, on the contrary, Father Païssy did once say something much like what you said... but of course it’s not the same, not at all the same,” Alyosha hastily corrected himself.

“A valuable admission, in spite of your ‘not at all the same.’ I ask you, why would your Jesuits and Inquisitors have united simply for vile material gain? Why can there not be among them one martyr, weighed down by great sorrow and loving humanity? Look, just suppose there was one such man among all those who want nothing but filthy material gain—just one like my old Inquisitor, who had himself eaten roots in the desert and made frenzied efforts to master his flesh so as to make himself free and perfect. Yet all his life he loved humanity, and suddenly his eyes were opened. He saw that there is no great moral blessedness in reaching perfection and freedom, if at the same time one becomes convinced that millions of God’s creatures have been made only as a mockery; that they will never be able to use their freedom; that these poor rebels can never turn into giants to finish the tower; and that it was not for such geese that the great idealist dreamed his dream of harmony. Seeing all that, he turned back and joined—the clever people. Surely that could have happened?”

“Joined whom? What clever people?” cried Alyosha, completely carried away. “They aren’t that clever, and they have no mysteries or secrets.... Perhaps nothing but atheism, that’s all their secret. Your Inquisitor doesn’t believe in God, that’s his secret!”

“So what if it is! You’ve finally guessed it. It’s perfectly true, that is the whole secret. But isn’t that suffering, at least for a man like him, who has thrown away his whole life in the desert and still could not shake off his incurable love for humanity? In his old age he arrived at a clear conviction: only the advice of the great, dread spirit could make any tolerable life for those feeble, unruly ‘incomplete, experimental creatures made as a joke.’ Convinced of this, he sees that he has to follow the counsel of the wise spirit, the dread spirit of death and destruction. So he has to accept lies and deception, and lead men knowingly to death and destruction, while deceiving them the whole way so that they never notice where they are being taken. That way the poor blind creatures can at least believe themselves happy on the road. And mark this: the deception is carried out in the name of Him Whose ideal the old man believed in so fervently all his life. Isn’t that tragic? And if just one such man stood at the head of the whole army ‘filled with the lust for power only for the sake of filthy gain,’ wouldn’t one be enough to make a tragedy? More than that, one such man at the head is enough to produce the true guiding idea of the Roman Church, with all its armies and Jesuits, its highest idea. I tell you frankly, I firmly believe there has always been a man like that among those at the head of the movement. Who knows, there may have been some even among the Roman Popes. Who knows, perhaps the spirit of that accursed old man, who loves mankind so obstinately in his own fashion, lives on right now in a whole crowd of such old men. They would exist not by chance but by agreement, as a secret league formed long ago to guard the mystery, to guard it from the weak and unhappy, in order to make them happy. No doubt that’s how it is, and how it has to be. I suspect even the Masons have something of the same mystery at bottom, and that’s why the Catholics hate the Masons so, as rivals who break up the unity of the idea, when it is so essential that there be one flock and one shepherd.... But the way I’m defending my idea, I might be an author who can’t take your criticism. Enough of that.”

“Maybe you’re a Mason yourself!” Alyosha blurted out. “You don’t believe in God,” he added, this time very sadly. He also thought his brother was looking at him with irony. “How does your poem end?” he asked, suddenly staring at the ground. “Or was that already the end?”

“This is how I meant to end it. When the Inquisitor finished speaking, he waited a while for his Prisoner to answer. The silence was heavy on him. He had seen that the Prisoner listened closely the whole time, gazing gently into his face, and clearly did not want to reply. The old man longed for Him to say something, however bitter and terrible. But He suddenly came up to the old man without a word and kissed him softly on his bloodless, aged lips. That was His whole answer. The old man shuddered. His lips moved. He went to the door, opened it, and said to Him: ‘Go, and come no more... do not come at all, never, never!’ And he let Him out into the dark alleys of the town. The Prisoner went away.”
“And the old man?”
“The kiss glows in his heart, but the old man sticks to his idea.”
“And you with him, you too?” cried Alyosha, mournfully.
Ivan laughed.

“Oh, it’s all nonsense, Alyosha. It’s just a senseless poem by a senseless student who never managed to write two lines of verse. Why take it so seriously? You can’t think I’m about to run off to the Jesuits and join the men who are correcting His work? Good Lord, that’s none of my business. I told you, all I want is to live on until thirty, and then... dash the cup to the ground!”

“But what about the little sticky leaves, and the precious graves, and the blue sky, and the woman you love? How will you live? How will you love them?” Alyosha cried sorrowfully. “With a hell like that in your heart and your head, how is it possible? No, that is just what you’re going away for, to join them... and if not, you’ll kill yourself. You can’t stand it!”
“There is a strength to bear anything,” Ivan said with a cold smile.
“What strength?”
“The strength of the Karamazovs—the strength of the Karamazov baseness.”
“To sink into debauchery, to stifle your soul with corruption, yes?”
“Possibly even that... only perhaps I’ll escape it until I’m thirty, and then—”
“How will you escape it? What will you escape it by? It’s impossible with your ideas.”
“In the Karamazov way, again.”
“‘Everything is lawful,’ you mean? Everything is lawful, is that it?”
Ivan scowled, and all at once turned strangely pale.

“Ah, you’ve picked up yesterday’s phrase, which so offended Miüsov—and which Dmitri pounced on so naïvely and put in his own words!” he smiled queerly. “Yes, if you like, ‘everything is lawful,’ since the words have been said. I won’t deny it. And Mitya’s version isn’t bad.”
Alyosha looked at him in silence.

“I thought that when I go away from here I would at least have you,” Ivan said suddenly, with unexpected feeling, “but now I see there is no place for me even in your heart, my dear hermit. The formula ‘all is lawful’ I won’t give up. Will you give me up for that, yes?”
Alyosha got up, went to him and softly kissed him on the lips.
“That’s plagiarism!” cried Ivan, highly pleased. “You stole that from my poem. Thanks anyway. Get up, Alyosha, it’s time we both left.”
They went out, but stopped when they reached the entrance of the restaurant.

“Listen, Alyosha,” Ivan began in a firm voice, “if I really can care for the sticky little leaves, I will love them only because I remember you. It’s enough for me that you are somewhere around, and I won’t lose my wish to live yet. Is that enough for you? Take it as a declaration of love, if you like. Now you go to the right and I to the left. And that’s all, do you hear, all. I mean that even if I don’t leave tomorrow (I think I certainly will) and we meet again, you are not to say one more word to me on these subjects. I ask that especially. And about Dmitri too, I ask you in particular, never speak to me of him again,” he added, with sudden irritation. “It’s all exhausted. It’s all been said over and over, hasn’t it? And I’ll make you one promise in return. When I reach thirty and want to ‘dash the cup to the ground,’ then wherever I am, I’ll come and have one more talk with you, even if I have to come from America. You can count on that. I’ll come on purpose. It will be very interesting to look at you and see what you’ve turned into by then. It’s a rather solemn promise, you see. And we really may be parting for seven years, or ten. Now go to your Pater Seraphicus. He is dying. If he dies while you’re not there, you’ll be angry with me for holding you up. Good-by. Kiss me once more, that’s right, now go.”

Ivan turned abruptly and walked off without looking back. It was just the way Dmitri had left Alyosha the day before, though that parting had been very different. The odd likeness flashed through Alyosha’s mind like an arrow, in the distress and dejection of that moment. He stood a little while, watching his brother go. Then he noticed that Ivan swayed as he walked, and that his right shoulder looked lower than his left. He had never noticed that before. But all at once he turned too and hurried, almost running, toward the monastery. It was nearly dark, and he felt almost afraid. Something new was growing in him, and he could not account for it. The wind had risen again, as on the evening before, and the ancient pines murmured gloomily around him as he entered the hermitage copse. He nearly ran. “Pater Seraphicus—he got that name from somewhere—where from?” Alyosha wondered. “Ivan, poor Ivan, and when shall I see you again?... Here is the hermitage. Yes, yes, that’s him, Pater Seraphicus, he will save me—from him and for ever!”

Several times afterward he wondered how, on leaving Ivan, he could have so completely forgotten his brother Dmitri, though that morning, only a few hours before, he had so firmly resolved to find him and not give up the search, even if he could not get back to the monastery that night.
